Theme

Playground equipment, sandbox toys, vehicles and play

chant verb and noun

words called over and over

classical

Ter. Ad. 4.7.32 (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Brut. 75: carmina in epulīs esse cantitāta (Lewis & Short)

cantitō, cantitāre, cantitāvī, cantitātum

verb, first conjugation

sing or chant over and over

Augustine’s word for the children’s sing-song from the house next door at Milan (Conf. 8.12.29).

Other words

  • dēcantō, dēcantāre, dēcantāvī, dēcantātum — keep repeating, chant

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.75 (Lewis & Short); Hor. Ep. 1.1.64

    Usually of something trite, said over and over (Lewis & Short).

  • nēnia, nēniae f. — a ditty, a children’s chant

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Hor. Ep. 1.1.62–63: puerōrum nēnia

    Chiefly a dirge (Cic., Hor.); Horace gives the name to the children’s chant of the king game.

Examples

  • at puerī lūdentēs: «rēx eris» ajunt, «sī rēctē faciēs»

    but the children in their game say, “You’ll be king if you do right”Hor. Ep. 1.1.59–60

  • utrumnam solērent puerī in aliquō genere lūdendī cantitāre tāle aliquid

    whether children used to chant anything like that in some gameAug. Conf. 8.12.29

See also chant, sing, song.
